IT IS A PLEASURE TO DISCUSS Esther Menaker's review of Lieberman's recently published biography on Otto Rank. Only in the last few years, after half a century of embarrassing neglect, Rank's original ideas and clinical understanding have been rediscovered. First our appreciation goes to Esther Menaker for reintroducing us to Rank in her excellent book (1982) and her many papers and lectures over the last decade. Now E. James Lieberman presents a partisan biography, but better researched and reasoned than Jessie Taft's (1958) study. Lieberman made extensive use of the Rank archives at Columbia University, and interviewed still-living colleagues, friends and relatives of Rank, to present a complex picture of Rank, the complex man, interwoven with Rank's ideas and the intensive interplay of prominent personalities in the history of the psychoanalytic movement.

Menaker highlights the major concepts of Rank, affirming Lieberman's excellent perspective. I would like to take a different tack. I have been teaching Rank for many years to psychoanalytic candidates, and certain issues have been asked consistently: Why study Rank? What influence did he have on the development of psychoanalysis in the United States? Where did Rank stand on controversies extant among psychoanalysts today?

One major tenet of psychoanalysis, ever since its inception has been that the past informs the present and the analyst can learn from that. Psychoanalysis has been devoted to the unfolding of lives—a living oral autobiography—ever-changing, in the intimacy of the patient-analyst dyad. The other group of professionals most concerned with the individual's total life are biographers (along with historians). We also adapt our psychoanalytic skills of examining meanings and motivations and have assessed historically the great psychoanalysts of our past. We thereby keep rewriting history, correcting distorted views and filling in the gaps of our knowledge with regard to our forefathers' ideas, and their clinical work. Lieberman's volume, however, is more than a biography of one man.

Introduction

IMRE HERMANN, THE GRAND old man of the Hungarian psychoanalytic movement, died February 22, 1984. He was 95 years old. With Sandor Ferenczi and Michael Balint he was representative of the so called "Budapest School of Psychoanalysis."

Hermann was graduated from the Medical School of Budapest University and began as a specialist in mental disorders. In his university years he attended one of Sandor Ferenczi's lectures on psychoanalysis. He soon became a passionate follower of the new science and a student of Ferenczi.

His first major works approached the psychology of thinking from the analytic point of view: Psychoanalyse und Logik (1924); Das Ich und das Denken (1929). A philosophical approach characterized his book entitled Psychoanalysis as a Method (1963), Psychoanalyse als Methode (1933).

From the early 1920s he paid close attention to the behaviour of primates and looked for biological analogies with psychoanalytic instinct theory in the lives of the apes closest to man. The results of twenty years of research were summed up in 1943 in his seminal work, 'Az ember ósi ösztönei' (The primitive instincts of man). This book, long unavailable in Hungary, was published in French and Italian a few years ago.

His greatest discovery, however, was the recognition of the clinging instinct, first published under the title, "Sich Anklammern-Auf Suche Gehen; Int. Zeitschr. Psa., 1936, 22: 349–370. (In English: "Clinging-going-in-search, " Psychoanal. Q., 1976, 45: 5–36.) He became aware of its existence in his study of the lives of apes: their young spend the first few months of their life holding on to their mothers' fur.

Lieberman, E. James, Acts of Will: The Life and Work of Otto Rank. New York: The Free Press, 1985.

THE PSYCHOANALYTIC MOVEMENT, like all movements—religious, political, social or philosophical—has never been kind to dissidents or revisionists. In the case of Otto Rank, who deviated from, and subsequently challenged much of Freudian theory, the Freudian establishment has been strikingly unkind. It has annihilated him with silence and has obliterated his name, much as an unkind parent might refuse to speak to a child who had misbehaved. Perhaps this is precisely because for twenty years Rank occupied a filial position in relation to Freud, so that his challenge to Freudian thought was experienced as disloyalty. "The little society [Freud's original, small group of disciples] acquired in him [Rank] a zealous and dependable secretary, and I gained in Otto Rank a faithful helper and co-worker, " wrote Freud. Rank was far from disloyal, but he was primarily true to his own perceptions and to his own thought. He was a man of his own will.

James Lieberman's book about Otto Rank is a well-researched, well-documented biography, even though, in Rank's case, it is especially difficult to separate the life of the man from his work. Perhaps this is so because the loneliness of Rank's early childhood, which then merged into a very conflictful adolescence, was perpetuated to some extent in the privacy of his personal and emotional life. Little is known about his feelings in personal relationships. His character and personality do emerge in his creative thinking and in the nature of his professional and semi-professional relationships. While there are passages in Lieberman's volume that poignantly reveal the depth and creativity of Rank's thinking, Acts of Will is not first and foremost a theoretical work. However, since before the appearance of this book relatively little had been written about Rank except for my own work, that of Jessie Taft and Fay Karpf, Lieberman's book is most welcome. It deals, as the subtitle indicates, with Rank's life and work, and in a calm and forthright manner with the controversial aspects of his life: the extent and nature of what has been promulgated as his emotional disturbance, the conflict with and separation from Freud, the relationship to Anais Nin and the cause of his death. Lieberman, through his non-adversarial approach, coupled with the presentation of factual data, sets the record straight, and transcends the mean and libelous mythology which has grown up around Rank's name.

THIS PAPER ADDRESSES THE observation that mental disorders are not fixed entities in the course of time.

Alex Comfort (1983) has written:

The context of psychiatry is existential: problems which perplex or disturb patients, however practical, are set in the context of how they perceive the human situation. So is the substance of psychiatry: how we practice it is bound on our ad hoc model of a world in which the phenomena of "mind" exist, however provisional this may be (p. 393).

Epidemiological and nosological data tend to change at various historical epochs. Neurotic symptoms, styles and fashions are influenced by prevailing socio-cultural models and prescriptions. The spirit of the times, i.e. "the Zeitgeist" seems to have a distinct impact on the overt manifestations of neurotic and some psychotic symptoms. It stands to reason that the forthcoming IVth edition of the APA: Diagnostic Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders will have difficulty keeping in step with changing models of neurosis. There are only fifteen years left of the 20th Century; the dawn of the 21st Century is not far away.

THE ROOTS OF A PERSON and of his ideas are to be found in his early formative personal experiences, and in the mediate culture to which he is later exposed. I can only note a few of the most salient biographical events which were major influences in Sullivan's development.

His life parallels that of the people he found a way to cure and, as Helen Swick Perry in her biography of Sullivan has shown, his life was the model for his theories. He grew up as the only surviving son of poor Irish Catholic parents, an outsider in a predominantly Protestant atmosphere. With a bitter mother, a detached father, and much parental turmoil, he was isolated in his family as well. Only one aunt seems to have had some understanding. He had to have had the early experience of feeling different in a shameful way. He knew loneliness well, and found solace as a brilliant physics student in high school, where he was befriended by the principal.

He went to Cornell, but failed in his first year. The following two years are completely unaccounted for, which has led to an undocumented belief that he might have had a breakdown and been hospitalized. In 1911, he was accepted at a third-rate medical school in Chicago. His medical training seems not to have been outstanding. However, he was exposed to the intellectual ferment and innovative thinking of the brilliant faculty at the University of Chicago at that time.

There was the sociologist George Herbert Mead, who had been a colleague of Charles Horton Cooley at the University of Michigan. Together they had done work on the development of the sense of self from the reflected appraisals of others, the so-called "mirror self", how one came to accept assigned roles. This was to have an important place in Sullivan's developmental theory.

There was the heritage of William James, the anti-dogmatic pragmatist, for whom truth was what worked; and John Dewey, espousing experience and education as a preparation for life.

TEACHING SULLIVAN'S INTERPERSONAL theory of psychiatry over a period exceeding three decades has been a learning experience of major proportions for me. In fact it had a distinctly personal impact on me, not dissimilar to being engaged in rewarding analytic therapy.

The "Preliminary Communication" co-authored by Freud and Breuer in 1893 is generally regarded as the first truly psychoanalytic publication; psychoanalysis as a discipline is therefore approaching its first centennial. Interpersonal Psychoanalysis, so fresh and radical in its reaction to the strictures of Freudian orthodoxy of the 1930's, is itself no longer new. It has endured, while many newer schools and closely related points of view have emerged around it: various theories of object relations, self psychology, recent developments in ego psychology, and so on. The very durability of Interpersonal Theory and its continued expansion within the proliferation of similar lines of theorizing raises difficult and complex questions for anyone interested in Interpersonal Psychoanalysis: What has been the historical impact and significance of Interpersonal Theory within psychoanalysis? What is its relation to other lines of thought? What can we say about its likely future course? The following three papers were part of a panel addressing these issues presented by the Manhattan Institute for Psychoanalysis on November 15, 1985.

OUR GROWING RESPECT FOR THE unconscious mind as the seat of creative thought has not yet come to the vital question of its role in discrimination and judgement. While we are ready to accept that the massive equipment of this unconscious mind may put before us its imaginative conjectures, in as many forms and from as many points of view of which it is capable, we are still prone to reserve for the function of consciousness, which, after all, we feel more to our credit and for which we are therefore more ready to accept responsibility, those finer functions which have to do with the correspondence of the hypothesis of meaning or significance to the evidence from observation that it is meant to cover or explain.

William Hazlitt in his "On the Knowledge of Character" wrote: "First impressions are often the truest, as we find (not infrequently) to our cost, when we have been wheedled out of them by plausible professions or studied actions. A man's look is the work of years, it is stamped on his countenance by the events of his whole life, nay, more, by the hand of nature, and it is not to be got rid of easily." Hazlitt seems often to be speaking of initial displeasure but his own madness of infatuation for his landlord's daughter reported in "Liber Amoris" commenced with a powerful first impression which subsequent events suggest may have been quite mistaken.

Similarly in describing the first meeting between Bouyard and Pecuchet, Flaubert writes: "Thus their meeting was important enough to be an adventure. They had at once become attracted by secret fibres. Besides, how can sympathies be explained? Why does some peculiarity, some imperfection, which would be indifferent or odious in one, seem enchanting in another? What is called the thunderbolt of love at first sight is true of all the passions."

It has often been said that by the age of forty a person has the face he deserves, leaving to the bloom of youth and the unlined face of early maturity a greater power of dis-simulation.

IAM INTERESTED IN THE BEHAVIORS and ways of relating which express the character traits we call hysterical. In my view, close examination of the interpersonal processes of hysterical engagement will clarify the development of hysterical pathology and lead to a clearer picture of the underlying psychic structure.

In what follows I will paint the picture of hysteria in broad strokes. It may appear I am describing the whole personality, or asserting all hysterical people are the same. I know this is not so. Each of the qualities I describe should be viewed on a continuum, ranging from deep pathology to normality. If I focus on the negative extreme, it is to clarify those underlying issues which are obscured in more subtle description. In hysterical fashion, I have chosen not to specify the diagnostic criteria of hysteria but will try to evoke interest in those qualities which give hysteria its flavor and style.

Furthermore, in my own thinking, I do not focus on the totality of the hysterical personality. I am interested in what I see as the mechanisms of hysteria—which in fact appear in all persons under the right conditions. In the throes of hysterical processes—laughing, crying, flirting, or telling a joke—any of us may illustrate the mechanisms I will describe, if only as a fraction of his personality.

The frustration of analytic technique and confusion of symptomatology in hysteria were first questioned by Marmor (1953). His hysterical patients showed mixed character traits and were not amenable to the rapid analytic cure predicted by the libidinal model. Sexuality, while flagrant, did not seem primary.

Probably every psycho-analyst would agree with the general statement that affects have a peculiarly intimate relation with instincts but that they are essentially ego-experiences. As Freud (1915) said years ago: "It is surely of the essence of an emotion that we should feel it, i.e., that it should enter consciousness". Further, we should probably agree that affects constitute a specific kind, or mode, of ego-experience; that they vary both in quality and quantity, and that individuals differ markedly both in the range and in the intensity of their affectivity. It is when we try to make these general statements more precise that we encounter difficulties. … We must have logical theory, but we do not work with theory, we work with living impulses and feelings. Hence, we should do well to check our theory by constant reference to our working experience of affects.— Marjorie Brierley

SOME PEOPLE ARE FATED to behold the face of death more than once. The sight is sprung upon them by cardiac arrests, accidents, and illnesses that have imperiled survival.

We might expect these people to tell us that the glimpse of death is harrowing, for many survivors are destined to suffer mental and emotional problems for the rest of their days. But what is true for these survivors is not true for all, for some find the experience of nearly dying to be an instigator to substantial changes that they and others view as beneficial.

We have found among the more favorably influenced survivors a small number who share several striking characteristics in addition to their common brushes with death. The personalities of members of this group of survivors change remarkably, and, of central concern to us in this paper, the changes evolve in tight association with novel experiences of self-understanding. These people become very curious about themselves, and they create special states of mind in which they find access to mutative experiences of self-knowing. They also tolerate the sense of uncertainty that openness to new knowing requires.

This group should hold compelling claims on our attention, because their changes bear striking resemblance to certain changes induced in people by psychoanalysis, particularly in the methods used to pursue self-knowledge. What is remarkable in these survivors is that they apparently grasp the nature of these methods in but a few moments of time—in fact, in the duration of the brush with death.

ALTHOUGH HE HAD BEEN USING the term for some years prior, Freud formally introduced the concept of narcissism into psychoanalytic theory in 1914 on the heels of Jung's painful defection from the psychoanalytic community. The theory of narcissism was largely a response to the conceptual challenge posed by Jung's critique of Freudian theory. Freud's libido theory had provided a powerful and compelling account of the various forms of neurosis, tracing them through complex associative pathways of transformation and disguise, to conflicts over libidinal wishes. Jung objected to what he felt was the narrowness of this account of human motivations, arguing that other kinds of issues, totally independent of sexuality, played a central role in mental health and psychopathology, particularly in psychotic disturbances such as schizophrenia. To meet Jung's challenge and to save his larger ambitions for libido theory, Freud had to account for schizophrenia in libidinal terms, to derive it interpretively from psychosexual wishes and conflicts.

In order to bring schizophrenia within the explanatory sway of libido theory, Freud expanded his view of the nature and developmental course of psychosexuality. Libido does not originate in the array of various infantile component instincts which Freud had unveiled beneath neurotic symptomatology. These various wishes constituting infantile psychosexuality are already a secondary phase in the course of libidinal development, in which libido has taken on objects in the external world. Prior to this turn outward, Freud argued, the totality of the infant's desire is directed towards the child's own self, discharged inwards.

EVER SINCE FREUD'S EPOCH making discoveries in the treatment of mental illness, which included the method of "free association", and an understanding of the Oedipus Complex, considerable attention has been paid to unconscious processes by psychologists. The interest which Freud sparked, however, has given rise to some widely shared misconceptions. Contrary to popular mythology, Freud did not discover the unconscious. Indeed, before the unconscious became a respectable topic for clinical investigation, it had been a matter for some considerable speculation by Leibniz and Kant, who approached it as a branch of epistemology, or what came to be known as Erkentnisstheorie.

Fortunately, the last few decades have witnessed the growth of a new literature intended to rectify this popular misconception. L. L. Whyte's The Unconscious Before Freud and Ellenberger's The Discovery of the Unconscious are merely two of the better known installments available to the general public. This being so, any attempt to canvass some of the same ground once more must furnish some plausible raison d'etre, or at least some basis in contemporary debate as its point of departure. Unfortunately, contemporary approaches to the relationship between the dynamic and cognitive unconscious are often oblivious to the historical background, notwithstanding the last few decades having witnessed a growing collaboration between cognitive theory and psychoanalysis, illustrated, for example, by the work of Rapaport, Peterfreund, Pribram and Gill, etc. (Pribram & Gill, 1976).

THIS PAPER CONSIDERS THE USE of pharmacotherapy in treatment as a special case of the general proposition that current psychoanalytic practice is characterized by movement away from the "classical" toward a more flexible psychoanalytic therapy. This flexibility consists of modifications in analytic procedure per se; and of adding to analytic procedures varying non-analytic modalities, such as behavioral methods and drug therapy. Short term dynamic psychotherapy is increasingly important as a modified psychoanalytic procedure.

Effective psychotropic medication was not available in the early years, but it is well known that Freud believed that biological, constitutional factors were an essential aspect of the person; and anticipated the future discoveries of chemical substances which would alter these biological factors. Winnicott (1947), (1960), Searles (1965), (1979), Sandler et al. Introduction

"I CAN IMAGINE AN INFANT", I sometimes feel it necessary to say, "held to two ample milky breasts—yet starving out of the pain of losing either, by choosing the one."

That this remark does not go down well (at least at first) can easily be imagined. The individuals to whom I make it feel deprived, empty. The idea of abundance is decidedly my own. Indeed my remark seems to them only to validate their experience: Is a comment like that supposed to help?

And yet, I feel persuaded that it does—that a long time ago, as now in the transference, there was a greed so great as to fail securely to metamorphose into appetite. Had it done so, such satisfactions as are available to the appetites might have consoled even compensated for the loss of the "other" breast. But in failing to give over into appetite, the greed, in its very nature insatiable and unsatisfiable, left a sequence of consequences that the analysis has somehow to put right.

In what follows I shall attempt to describe these consequences and the matter of helping put them right. But in doing so I shall be venturing onto the treacherous shoals of originology on which psychoanalysis so often founders.

In the consulting room a remark such as mine about the infant and the breasts can be taken either (or both) as metaphor or construction of historical experience. Its validity is moot; only its usefulness matters.

THE THERAPEUTIC STANCE THAT is referred to as neutral is designed to protect the patient and the therapeutic situation. It is an effort to structure into the therapeutic process a nonjudgmental frame of mind. MY ASSUMPTION IS THAT THE question we are addressing: Where does a given analyst place him or herself on a continuum "from neutrality to personal revelation?" is more than definitional or idiosyncratically preferential. Rather it is a question about a dynamic issue—the answers being governed by principles or formulations the analyst follows.

I shall discuss the effect of two working principles on the tension between revelation and non-revelation. The first—the nature of the analytic exchange presses toward revelation. The second—the analyst's systematic use of the empathic mode of perception presses toward carefully circumscribing the nature of the revelation.

Let me describe my view of analysis. Analyst and analysand come together to effect a positive change in the analysand (with emphasis on the relief of psychic distress, conscious and unconscious) through understanding in depth the nature of some problem or problems. Analyst and analysand, however, have different perspectives that lead inevitably to different motives; each is consequently under strains that as they interact provide the treatment's major dynamic leverage.

From the analysand's side: He or she will be under all the tensions brought to the analysis as a result of the accumulation of unresolved regulatory disturbances and conflicts from the past. In each analytic session, the analysand will feel pulled toward an internally obligatory full expression of his or her perceived needs and wishes. This sense of "immediate demand" is an analytically necessary part of the experience. AMONG THE MANY IMPORTANT and fruitful ideas which Sullivan developed, the concept I have found most important in broadening my own perspective and stimulating my own thinking has been the notion of the interpersonal field. The way an observer approaches and defines the object of study, Sullivan argued, goes a long way in determining what sort of data he will come up with and how he will account for them.

For Freud, the object of study in psychopathology is the individual mind. His "intrapsychic" model traces neurotic symptoms back to processes and structures arising within the mind of the patient. Sullivan felt that Freud had incorrectly framed the phenomena in question. Psychopathology is best approached, Sullivan believed, not in terms of one person, but in the context of actual interactions among persons, in terms of what he called the "interpersonal field." Personality and psychopathology do not exist in germinal form within the child, simply unfolding as a bud into a blossom; personality and psychopathology derive from, are composed of, interactions between the child and significant others. To understand the person in a meaningful way, you have to view the person in the context of the field from which he or she emerged and operates.

In my view, this illuminating approach to persons is also usefully applied to the history of ideas.

Introduction

THIS ESSAY IS INTENDED TO develop further and explicate a characterology of psychoanalytic self psychology. As with all character studies it should be seen as highlighting traits that are ubiquitous to some degree in the entire population, while outstanding in some few individuals. It is thus to be considered as a lifelong pattern of behavior which in turn is tied to normal development. This linkage should not be seen as connecting a specific time of occurrence, but rather as one denoting a certain enduring quality of relationships. We may see the self through life as having qualities of coherence, firmness, harmony, continuity, etc. This last point, that of a feeling of sameness through time and space, will be focused upon as crucial to the emergence of the particular character to be considered here. In a previous paper on the misfit, the developmental difficulty of that pattern was noted to be a failure to achieve a necessary transition from one stage to the next because of the lack of sustaining selfobjects at the succeeding stage. The present cohort of patients is differentiated on the basis of the failed sense of stability which would allow such a transit to be even considered. In a simplified way this would translate to the wishy-washy person showing a defect earlier than the misfit, but such a simplification should not be read as being time-bound, e.g., the first at 13 months and the next at 21 or as reflecting severity of pathology. Since we see that people need stability and responsiveness throughout life, we should be able to highlight a character disorder that reflects the problematic state of these needs. The one that is selected here for examination is that of self-continuity. Once again it is necessary to examine this sort of organization primarily in terms of the emerging transference manifestations and not at all in a phenomenological or descriptive sense of social relationships, although these may conform to what is ultimately to be the prevalent transference.

I APPRECIATE AND RESPECT WHAT Dr. Bromberg has to say and see hardly any point with which I would seriously dissent. There are perhaps a few which I should like to clarify. In the main, I shall refrain from any defense about my conduct of the case since this is a very abbreviated version of an intense experience, and all of the suggestions about alternate interpretations and/or countertransference issues are well taken.

Self psychology struggles hard not to be an interpersonal psychology not only because it wishes to avoid the social psychological connotations of the phrase but also because it wishes to minimize the input of the analyst into the mix. We certainly see that this is unavoidable and thus constantly strive to scrutinize our input. It is not minimized merely to keep the field pure so much as to allow a thwarted development to unfold. Since self psychology is so preeminently a developmental psychology, it is based on the idea of a developmental program (one that may be innate or pre-wired if you wish) that will reconstitute itself under certain conditions. Now the conditions will vary, and thus the results will not be uniform, but the program remains one determined and directed by the patient. The analyst serves as selfobject to the patient and interprets these heterogeneous functions rather than the patient serving as selfobject to the analyst and thus substituting action for interpretation.

ON 5TH JUNE 1985 THE British Psycho-Analytical Society held a Symposium on Projective Idenfication. During the discussion Hanna Segal pointed out that the analyst is in no position to interpret if the interpretation is based only upon what the analyst is feeling in the session. Unless it is possible to identify how the patient is contributing to what the analyst is feeling, and in such a way that the patient could recognize this, then it is better to remain silent.

It is, of course, essential that the analyst not interpret simply on the basis of what he is feeling—that amounts to magical understanding of the patient. Some patients actually will welcome this kind of intervention because it gratifies their passivity and their wishes to be drawn into a state of merging with the analyst. Other patients, however, will experience it as omnipotent, intrusive and persecutory.

One of the most significant shifts in psychoanalytic technique, in the past forty years, has developed from the changing attitudes to countertransference and from the diagnostic significance attributed to the analyst's affective responses to the patient (Winnicott, 1947) ; (Heimann, 1950) ; (Little, 1951) ; (King, 1978) ; (Epstein and Feiner, 1979).

During this period of time the process of projective identification has come to be seen as a means whereby unmanageable affects are communicated to another person. An unconscious hope is implied in this process, that the recipient may be better able to manage being in touch with these difficult feelings than the person seeking to "get rid of" them (Bion, 1967) ; (Rosenfeld, 1971) ; (Grotstein, 1981) ; (Ogden, 1982) ; (Casement, 1985).

FEW ISSUES IN PSYCHOANALYSIS are quite so muddled, or tend to generate quite so much confusion in the mind of the clinician, as the relationship between theory and technique. There are many reasons for this, all related in one way or another to the poor match between the kind of work that theory-making is, and the kind of work that clinical practice is. One aspect of this is the inescapable but jarring mismatch between an activity which is inherently public and one which is fundamentally private. Theorizing, necessarily, is done publicly. Theoretical contributions by their nature must be written down or spoken aloud. When they are debated, all participants have access to what is said, if not necessarily to what is meant. Technique, on the other hand, is obviously private. There exists no record of all the transactions constituting an analysis, nor could such a record exist, even in principle.

Because of this, the translation of theoretical principles into technical precepts eludes outside observation. Theory applied is, inevitably, theory interpreted. Personal predilection gives the application an idiosyncratic, and decisive, cast. By the time it is run through the analyst's particular vision of human life, not to mention his personality, the impact of theory is difficult to trace.

SINCE ITS INCEPTION SOME sixteen years ago, the communicative approach has insisted upon a highly definitive listening and formulating process in the therapeutic situation. In particular, the approach has maintained a sharp distinction between derivative (encoded or transformed) and nonderivative (unencoded) communications from patients. This has led to a stress on the distinction between conscious and unconscious communication, and to the realization that the latter is central to the unconscious basis of madness—a term used here in its broadest possible sense to refer to all forms of psychopathology, intrapsychic and interpersonal, psychological and somatic.

The basic listening process adopted by the communicative approach consistently applied Freud's (1900) paradigm of the stimulus-response model that accounts for dream formation (though the present approach recognized the circularity or system aspects, the interactional component of stimulus evocation, feedback, feed forward, and mutual influence). Thus, the communicative approach drew strength from what is in all likelihood Freud's greatest discovery, namely, that human beings have two ways of thinking—one that takes place in terms of secondary process functioning and the other which follows the rules of the primary processes.

IN Madness and Cure, ROBERT LANGS PRESENTS the reader with an empirically-based companion volume to his last book, The Psychotherapeutic Conspiracy. (Langs, 1982a) Both books are attempts to illustrate Langs' concept of therapeutic collusion, the Conspiracy volume on a macro- or sociological level, and the Madness volume on the level of micro- or individual analysis.

In Madness and Cure, Langs asks why patients claim cure in therapies that neither confront nor interpret the symbolism of unconscious mental processes. Freud demonstrated very clearly that unraveling the unconscious meaning of various emotional disorders was the soundest basis for the cure of emotionally-founded disorders. Langs demonstrates how cure is claimed and sought in psychotherapies that provide gratification through avoidance of anxiety that would otherwise trigger the disturbing meanings of the patient's illness. In a similar vein, the patient's efforts and need to cure the therapist serve to keep the patient in a collusive therapy. The therapist's lack of suitable boundaries is often a significant factor in therapies that encourage action-discharge modes of cure instead of genuine insight and working through methods. This lack of boundaries may signal to the patient that the therapist needs his or her help.

In one rather sad case, the former patient of a therapist who had attempted to seduce her after having had sexual affairs with two of her friends, also patients of this therapist, was turned away by members of her therapy group. Roberta Held-Weiss, Ph.D.

ROBERTA HELD-WEISS DIED OCTOBER 4, 1985. She was 51 years old. She had had a short but distinguished career as a psychoanalyst, first as candidate at the William Alanson White Institute, then as graduate, supervising analyst and supervisor of psychotherapy, and as a member of the teaching faculty. She had joined the staff of This Journal recently, and her name appeared, for the first time, on the mast head of the October, 1985 issue. She once wrote (1985)1:

(What) we look for in psychoanalysis is not to be found while searching for historical events or causes, nor in recreating, restoring, or repairing the past. Neither would I locate it in a hermeneutic exegesis, a coherent and logical narrative. Instead I would search for it in our patients' struggle to give shape and meaning to their experience, in their efforts, however fragmented, unordered, incoherent, desultory, erratic or formless these efforts may be. Psychoanalytic truth … emerges in the analysis of the immediate analytic experience, in the observation and analysis of the participation. That is, it is in a reflection on its own process, in a self-consciousness of the emerging experience between the analyst and patient, continually being redefined … This is not to preclude the study of lives, or for that matter, the patient's experience of the past, as it gets actualized, articulated in, and filtered through the present (pp. 237–238).

She had many friends, the relationships with whom she nurtured, and kept intensely for many years, a loving family to whom she was devoted, and the respect of her classmates and teachers, who considered her a colleague. She is mourned by all.

Introduction

SOME OF US WILL, OF COURSE, reflect with high hopes upon the possible implications that exciting achievements in neuroscience have for the convergence of neuroscience and psychoanalysis. But why should we anticipate such a convergence? Do we foresee a solution to the mind-body problem? Is the theoretical reducibility of psychoanalysis by neuroscience within our reach? Do the contributions made by neuroscience to the explanation and treatment of psychopathology increasingly replace and render obsolete those contributions made by psychoanalysis?

In this paper, I shall advance arguments for five positions, which here, in introduction, I merely assert.

1. The mind-body problem, as it is usually stated, is a metaphysical problem. Insofar as it is stated as a metaphysical problem, no empirical evidence can contribute to its solution.

2. If we want answers to our questions about the relation between mind and body that are dependent upon and responsive to empirical knowledge, then the mind-body problem is best conceived as a question about the relation between two scientific disciplines. More specifically, it is best conceived as a question about the relation between the theories of a psychology of mind and the theories of neuroscience.

IN THIS PAPER, I WOULD LIKE to assess the impact of J. J. Bachofen and matriarchal theory on four important psychoanalytic theoreticians. Although this sort of topic is seldom addressed with much energy or enthusiasm anymore, one thing that strikes the psychoanalytic historian is the way in which, among the early pioneers, clinical theory informed, and was, in turn informed by, a wide network of interlacing assumptions about social, historical and intrapsychic reality, in which the nature and meaning of religion figure prominently. The first hint that this is so is possibly in The Psychopathology of Everyday Life, in which Freud declared that religious mythology represents an alienated apperception of intrapsychic processes, which are destined to be unravelled by the psychology of the unconscious (Freud, 1901). Although sharing in this fundamental assumption, Freud's dissident followers espoused different philosophical anthropologies and different philosophies of history, as expressed in their clinical orientations as well as their cultural writings. Due to the essentially comparative nature of this inquiry, I can not do justice to any individual theorist's output. Moreover, as Jung, Rank, Fromm, and indirectly, Ian Suttie, were all influenced by Bachofen, I have allowed myself to wander somewhat across the historical landscape to make appropriate interpolations and juxtapositions, so as to put Bachofen's influence in proper historical perspective.

TWO RECENT WORKS HAVE SOUGHT to clarify the distinction between the intrapsychic and the interpersonal approaches to psychoanalysis. Greenberg and Mitchell (1983) see each approach as embodying a major tradition in Western philosophy. The intrapsychic model embraces as its fundamental premise the notion that the individual mind is the most meaningful unit of study. The interpersonal model begins from the idea that human beings are essentially social.

Levenson (1983) has drawn this distinction in terms of each model's approach to reality. The European-based intrapsychic model conceives of reality as a springboard for an autonomous, internally driven fantasy process. The interpersonal model, as conceived by Sullivan (1953), views the patient as disabled by an uncomprehended reality, not by an anachronistic fantasy system. That is, the interpersonal analyst of the "American pragmatic psychoanalytic movement" (Levenson, 1983, p. 11) is interested in the difficulties a person has in realizing a meaningful reality, in the sense of what Levenson describes as a "semiotic competence." This is in contrast to the interpersonal analyst who uses an intrapsychic model, and locates the meaning gap between an internally driven fantasy and an external reality.

In making this distinction, Levenson stresses that an interpersonal approach can embrace either view. That is; if one adopts the interpersonal perspective of an object-relations model of psychoanalysis—as is done by W. R. D. Fairbairn (1952), and D. W. Winnicott (1958) —one sees the patient as disabled by an anachronistic fantasy system.

THE PERSONAL, THE IDIOSYNCRATIC, the spontaneous, the unpredictable aspects of the analyst's experience remain outside of the realm of the acceptable and are unappreciated for their positive contribution to the analytic work.

The study of the value of analytic neutrality and anonymity has been carried out, but the value of the spontaneous and unpredictable hasn't been integrated into our self image. It remains outside the body of technique and will always be so. There is more to analysis than interpretation—correct, penetrating and well timed; yet attention is not usually drawn specifically to this aspect of our effort. The analytic material or context is to be understood and interpreted, subject to objective, detached and impersonal observation. In contrast we casually refer to the implicit, the tacit connectedness of the relationship, the working alliance or the analytic setting. ONLY APPROXIMATELY FIVE PERCENT OF individuals who suffer a massive coronary occlusion survive through artificial resuscitation procedures. The authors review some of the literature describing these survivors and report that more than one-third experience a new-found and enduring sudden understanding or insight. The experience often is one of being outside of oneself, observing the frantic scene "below, " of light, of vivid review of one's life, and is an ineffable experience of being taken up and held by a gigantic being. The authors have, in addition, interviewed nineteen such individuals, a few of whom have an enduring new-found self-curiosity. To my knowledge, the authors report, for the first time, an instance in which a recovered individual then has sought psychoanalytic treatment. He sought treatment for perhaps the optimal reason: to continue and deepen an experience of intense quest for knowledge, specifically self-knowledge, out of a newly-discovered sense that his pre-cardiac-arrest personality had been encumbered by neurotic illness. This insight, more usually the hard-won result of an effective psychoanalytic treatment, was the motivating factor in seeking analysis. In addition, the authors feel that this patient first grasped the nature of psychoanalytic method during the brush with death.

DR. LIONELLS' PAPER MAKES US reconsider some basic issues about diagnostic entities and approaches to treatment. She has changed the focus from understanding the libidinal conflicts underlying hysterical symptom formation, to how the hysteric relates to the significant people in his life. This is, of course, the interpersonal approach to analysis (Sullivan, 1954). She challenges the usefulness of studying symptoms to understand hysteria, arguing that many authors have observed "hysterical" symptoms in a variety of diagnostic groups. My own research on agoraphobia (supposedly a form of anxiety hysteria) also indicated that this symptom appeared in a wide range of diagnostic types. I would agree therefore that understanding the dynamics of a symptom is not the best way to understand, and help the patient.
